articles.title: Slow Oscillations Modulate Overnight Brain Changes in Working Memory Function
articles.content: Working memory (WM), the transient storage and manipulation of information, is a cognitive function that can improve with training. Accumulating evidence suggests that sleep, particularly slow oscillations (SOs) that occur during nonrapid eye movement sleep, supports this improvement. Yet, how sleep and SOs in particular relate to neural processes supporting WM remains poorly understood. In this study, we investigated how WM-related neural activity evolves across nocturnal sleep and how these changes relate to neural processing during SOs. Participants performed a WM task during fMRI before and after sleep, with simultaneous EEG–fMRI capturing neural activity during the first 2.5 hr of sleep. Our results showed significant overnight changes in WM-related activity, characterized by reduced recruitment of the dorsal precuneus during WM encoding/maintenance phases and frontal regions during the retrieval phase of WM. In addition, sleep increased item-specific reinstatement in a sensory processing region during WM. This pattern of results suggests a combined influence of sleep on enhancing sensory reinstatement while reducing potential top–down control (i.e., reduced parietal and frontal activity). Critically, SO-related activity was directly linked to overnight activity changes: Stronger SO activation in the premotor cortex and ventromedial pFC predicted greater overnight reductions in WM-related activity, and multivoxel analyses in the ventral attention network revealed a parallel relationship. These findings suggest that SOs play a critical role in WM function by facilitating the reorganization of WM-related processing.

articles.title: Transformer Mechanisms Mimic Frontostriatal Gating Operations When Trained on Human Working Memory Tasks
articles.content: Working memory (WM) is thought to rely on sophisticated frontostriatal mechanisms for selective gating, supporting updating and readout of information to and from distinct memory “addresses” (neural populations). According to computational models, capacity limitations in WM arise due to challenges in “role addressability”: learning to correctly bind items in memory to their respective roles and assigning credit to the corresponding gating operations. However, these conclusions are based on particular assumptions about biological neural networks, and it is unclear whether the principles generalize to other architectures. To address this question, we examine whether similar gating mechanisms emerge in Transformer neural network architectures, which have demonstrated success on tasks requiring executive function—the ability to represent, coordinate, and manage multiple subtasks—yet lack intentionally built-in gating mechanisms. We analyze the mechanisms that emerge within Transformers trained on human WM tasks explicitly designed to place demands on gating. We find that the Transformer's attention mechanism develops role-addressable input and output gating, but only when trained on task distributions that benefit from frontostriatal-like gating mechanisms. Moreover, these gating strategies support enhanced generalization and variable binding and increase the models' effective capacity to store and access multiple items in memory, resembling the constraints found in frontostriatal models. These results suggest that gating mechanisms serve a fundamental computational role in managing role addressability and binding and highlight opportunities for future research on computational similarities between modern artificial intelligence architectures and models of the human brain.

articles.title: Visual Perspective Shapes Subjective Experience: Dissociable Parietal Contributions to the Constructive Nature of Memory
articles.content: Subjective features of memory are often treated as secondary to the objective content of remembered events. However, growing evidence suggests that these features actively shape how memories are constructed, experienced, and used. Rather than treating visual perspective as a peripheral correlate of subjectivity, this review positions it as a key mechanism that shapes the memory. Because perspective can be flexibly controlled and reliably measured, it offers a unique window into how retrieval goals interact with mental simulation to produce vivid and emotionally resonant recollections. Drawing on behavioral and neuroimaging research, this review shows that visual perspective determines the spatial framing of memory and the emotional and sensory qualities of recollection. Focusing on the posterior parietal cortex, it outlines distinct roles for the angular gyrus (AG) and the precuneus in supporting perspective-dependent retrieval. The AG contributes to the selection and maintenance of a retrieval perspective, integrating perceptual and conceptual features into a coherent scene. In contrast, the precuneus supports spatial transformation and modulates the vividness, emotional tone, and embodied character of recollection, particularly when individuals recall events from a nondominant or shifted perspective. Together, these findings position visual perspective as a central mechanism in the construction of subjectivity. Understanding how perspective shapes the process of remembering provides insight into how memory supports emotion regulation, mental simulation, and the continuity of the self across time.

articles.title: Memory Traces Reflect How They Were Last Accessed
articles.content: Episodic memories are known to change with each act of retrieval. We hypothesize that accessing semantic knowledge in different ways during episodic retrieval—from unique perceptual features to taxonomic and thematic context—shapes how those memories are subsequently represented during recognition. In this fMRI study, human participants learned novel word–image pairs and underwent re-exposure that required accessing semantic knowledge at one of three different levels: item, category, or theme. Participants then completed a recognition task. Although behavioral memory performance was matched across conditions, neural activity during recognition varied based on prior semantic access history. Recognition patterns could be classified according to prior semantic access in early visual cortex, ventral temporal cortex, and the hippocampus for remembered concepts. A whole-brain searchlight analysis revealed bilateral clusters along the ventral visual stream where semantic access history was decodable. To further characterize how prior semantic access history shaped neural representations during recognition, we tested whether memories accessed at the same semantic level were expressed more similarly or distinctly in the brain. Category-level access increased similarity among items in early visual cortex, whereas item-level access led to more differentiated representations in the visual word form area. Together, these findings show that how we access semantic knowledge during episodic retrieval leaves measurable traces in subsequent neural representations, revealing how semantic–episodic interactions shape memory representations.

articles.title: The Temporal Dynamics of Attentional Allocation during Counterfactual Learning
articles.content: Counterfactual learning, the ability to learn from what could have happened under different circumstances, is a key cognitive mechanism supporting behavioral adaptation. While its neural and computational underpinnings are increasingly understood, the temporal dynamics of attention toward factual and counterfactual outcomes remain poorly characterized. Here, we investigate the biological mechanisms underlying this process using a reinforcement learning task combined with eye-tracking and pupillometry in 36 human participants. Participants completed a two-armed bandit task with full outcome feedback and exhibited a robust confirmation bias, learning more from outcomes that supported their previous choices. Gaze patterns revealed a consistent temporal sequence of fixations from factual to counterfactual outcomes, modulated in opposite directions by the valence of each outcome. Pupil dilation, a proxy for noradrenergic arousal, was influenced by the factual outcome and by the similarity between factual and counterfactual feedback, consistent with increased surprise during disconfirmatory events. These results provide a mechanistic account of how attentional and arousal systems jointly shape outcome evaluation. By integrating behavioral modeling with physiological markers, this work contributes to a broader understanding of the adaptive constraints on decision-making and offers new insight into how organisms evaluate hypothetical alternatives in learning contexts.

articles.title: Theta and High-alpha Phase-locking Dynamics Unveil Face Perception in Ambiguous Stimuli
articles.content: Previous studies emphasize phase synchronization as a fundamental mechanism for integrating local features into coherent percepts. We employed a novel paradigm and dynamic graph analysis based on EEG to track neural dynamics associated with perceiving a face (or not) while keeping the stimuli identical. Thirty participants underwent a pretest to establish perceptual thresholds for detecting faces within images overlaid with visual noise. These thresholds were then applied in an EEG experiment with the same task, focusing on images with 50% and 75% detection probabilities. In the high-alpha band, we observed increased coupling (100–275 msec after stimulus onset) between the left and right occipitotemporal electrodes when an ambiguous stimulus was perceived as a face, indicating conscious face perception. The failure to perceive a face resulted in enhanced theta band phase synchronization between bilateral occipitotemporal electrodes and increased high-alpha-band coupling between the left frontal and right occipitotemporal electrodes, which showed face-selective responses. These synchronizations are likely to reflect the continuous gathering of individual bits of facial information rather than signaling the presence or absence of a face percept. Additionally, we identified frontal–occipitotemporal theta-band couplings related to the stimulus’s informational content, irrespective of whether the inherent face was perceived. Our findings reveal distinct temporal dynamics in phase synchronization at specific frequencies, indicating a specialized system for face perception during integrated information processing across the frontal and visual cortex, resolving ambiguities.

articles.title: Capturing the Attentional Trade-off between Speech Planning and Comprehension
articles.content: In conversation, future speakers often plan speech simultaneously with comprehension, which means that they must divide attentional resources between these processes. In this EEG study, we used responses to linguistic attention probes (i.e., syllable “BA” presented during spoken sentences) to track temporal variations in attention to comprehension. Participants were asked to listen to prerecorded sentences with expected or unexpected sentence-final words. Each sentence was presented twice, once with and once without the attention probe starting 100 msec after the target word onset. Participants saw a picture 50 msec before the target word. Depending on the test block (picture naming or button press), participants either named the picture or pressed the space bar, both after an 850-msec delay. The probes elicited a negative potential approximately 100 msec after probe onset (i.e., an attention probe effect) in all probe conditions. Unexpectedly, neither word expectancy nor speech planning influenced the timing or strength of the attention probe effect. This indicates that expectancy of words in Dutch does not affect the allocation of attention toward these words 100 msec after their onset (i.e., the time of the probe presentation). Interestingly, engaging in speech planning does not seem to divert attentional resources away from comprehension at the moment of probe presentation. These findings imply that listeners are able to effectively distribute their attentional resources between comprehension and speech planning and carry out these processes at the same time. Considering these unexpected findings, using attention probes might not be the best approach to capture variations in temporal attention in dual-task paradigms.

articles.title: Sampling the Training Trajectory of Vision Models Reveals a Mismatch with Human Visual Development
articles.content: We compare time-resolved EEG representational geometry across seven age groups, from 6 months to adulthood, with representations sampled throughout training from supervised and self-supervised ResNet-50 and ViT-B/16. Previous model-brain comparisons mostly used adult brain recordings and untrained or fully trained networks. We find that successive training stages do not systematically progress from child- to adult-like neural representations: alignment with every age group from 4 years onward emerges early in training and remains stable. Training adds substantial alignment beyond the untrained architecture, similarly at every age. Finally, categorical structure and spatial frequency each explain a stable share of the neural geometry at every age, with apparent age-related increases in categorical organization reflecting increased EEG reliability. Because standard training on full-resolution images aligns with all ages early, and spatial frequency, which depends on maturing visual acuity, strongly shapes the neural geometry, developmentally structured visual input may help models follow human visual development.

articles.title: Does Denoising Reduce Cross-Vendor Variability in Diffusion MRI? A Travelling Heads Evaluation
articles.content: Between-scanner variability in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-derived features can be comparable to biological between-subject variability, even for the same individual scanned at different sites. MRI harmonisation is therefore an essential tool to ensure studies are generalisable across sites, reducing between-scanner variability and enabling pooling of data to achieve large sample sizes and more representative population samples. Denoising using MPPCA is widely used in preprocessing pipelines for diffusion MRI acquisitions to improve image SNR and it has been proposed as an implicit way of harmonising data. In this registered report, we hypothesised that denoising reduces cross-scanner variability and improves reliability in diffusion MRI metrics without changing cross-scanner bias, and that susceptibility-induced off-resonance reduces its efficacy. We tested these hypotheses using a travelling-heads resource of ten subjects scanned on six scanners from three vendors (GE, Philips, Siemens), with within-scanner repeats. We found that: i) Denoising reduced voxel-wise cross-scanner coefficients of variation for fractional anisotropy (FA), mean diffusivity (MD) and mean kurtosis (MK) (BF > 100; median -3%, -9% and -32%). ROI-wise, variability decreased for MK (-12%), increased for FA (+8%), and evidence was inconclusive for MD. ii) Contrary to our hypothesis, denoising changed cross-scanner bias in every subject-scanner pair, by up to 3% of the mean; in exploratory analyses, this change was strongly related to contrast-to-noise ratio. iii) Evidence for a change in the registered measure of reliability was inconclusive, although exploratory analyses showed higher voxel-wise reliability after denoising. iv) There was no convincing evidence that off-resonance reduces denoising efficacy. Together, these results suggest that MPPCA denoising reduces the random, noise-driven component of cross-scanner variability, most strongly at the voxel level and for kurtosis, but does not consistently reduce systematic differences between scanners. As such, it should complement harmonisation, not replace it.
articles.author: D'Antonio, F., Manzano Patron, J. P., Mougin, O., Morgan, P. S., Sotiropoulos, S., Warrington, S.

articles.title: Jump: Making Large-Scale Connectomics Accessible
articles.content: Large-scale connectomic resources generated from volumetric electron microscopy (EM) have transformed neuroscience by enabling detailed 3D reconstructions of cellular and subcellular morphology and connectivity across hundreds of thousands of cells in diverse tissues and organisms. Recent advances in machine learning-based cell classification and automated segmentation have enabled large-scale annotation of these datasets, yet barriers remain in validating automated classifications and extracting biological insights. To address these challenges, we developed Jump, a suite of user-friendly web-based platforms generated using Claude. These platforms support interactive exploration, expert-guided community review, and quantitative analysis of multiple publicly available EM datasets, while building a growing repository of community-generated annotations. Using uJump, which hosts data from the MICrONS mouse visual cortex dataset, as an example, we demonstrate rapid retrieval of specific cell populations, region-of-interest filtering, biological inspection of cells, and extraction of quantitative morphological and spatial metrics. We showcase analytical features including cell abundance and spatial organisation, connectivity, local cellular neighbourhoods, and volumetric measurements. Using pericytes and endothelial cells as a case study on the cortical vasculature, we further demonstrate how manual review and reclassification can generate accurately identified cell populations for downstream analyses. Consistent with the open-science principles underpinning many large-scale EM resources, Jump is designed to enable broad community participation. By lowering technical barriers to the use of EM datasets, Jump increases analytical efficiency and promotes collaborative efforts to accurately classify cells and structures. Expert-reviewed annotations can be shared across the community, allowing users to build on existing work rather than repeatedly validating the same automated classifications. Collectively, Jump will help researchers to accelerate biological discovery from connectomic datasets.
articles.author: Morris, G. P., Mohamed, H. F., Selim, R. S., Eyo, U., Bonney, S. K., Mughal, A., Grubb, S.

articles.title: Childhood Trauma Severity Compounds Reward Anticipation Disruption in Substance Use Disorders
articles.content: Background: Substance use disorders (SUD) are associated with reward circuit disruptions and high rates of trauma. Trauma has been found to reduce propensity to engage frontal, limbic, and striatal regions during reward anticipation. However, the interactive effect of trauma and SUD on anticipatory reward circuitry remains unclear. Methods: To address this critical research gap, treatment-enrolled individuals with at least one SUD (N = 150; 78 female) completed questionnaires assessing childhood trauma and current posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms and a monetary incentive delay (MID) task during functional magnetic resonance imaging. The MID task presented participants with cues predicting the delivery of no, small, and large monetary gains and avoidance of equally weighted losses. Linear mixed effects models examined the effect of trauma severity or PTSD on percent signal change for anticipation of monetary gains, extracted from a-priori striatal, prefrontal, and mesolimbic anatomic regions of interest. Results: 70.7% of individuals experienced significant childhood trauma and 63.3% met self-report symptom thresholds for probable PTSD. Current PTSD symptoms were positively associated with emotion dysregulation, emotional impulsivity, and drug craving, but were not related to anticipatory BOLD signal. Higher childhood trauma severity (but not current PTSD severity) was associated with lower anticipatory responses within the nucleus accumbens, caudate, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and anterior insula to both gain and loss cues. Conclusions: Childhood adversity is associated with blunted reward anticipation across striatal, prefrontal, and limbic circuitry. This highlights the importance of considering childhood trauma severity in SUD treatment, which may require targeted interventions beyond standard cognitive behavioral therapy to restore normative salience processing, such as striatal neuromodulation.
articles.author: Aguilar, S. A., Qundes, S. I., Kuplicki, R., Aupperle, R. L., Stewart, J. L., Gueguen, M. C. M.

articles.title: Discovery of latent clinical phenotypes through optimal transport of brain dynamics
articles.content: The increasing availability of large clinical neuroimaging datasets has enabled the discovery of objective, data-driven clinical phenotypes. However, current approaches typically rely on structural or static functional metrics, thereby overlooking the rich information embedded in brain dynamics. To address this limitation, we developed a computational framework combining a Gaussian Hidden Markov Model (HMM) with Optimal Transport (OT) theory. By representing individual brain dynamics within a shared latent state space, our approach quantifies how much one subject's state-transition dynamics would need to be modified to match another subject's state occupancy distribution, providing a pairwise measure of inter-individual variability that captures temporal aspects of brain function. We applied this framework to multiple sclerosis (MS), a condition where substantial within-group heterogeneity challenges traditional clinical classification. Analyzing resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 122 patients with relapsing-remitting MS and 97 matched healthy controls, the HMM identified three latent states with distinct connectivity patterns. While patients showed an altered temporal organization of recurrent brain states relative to healthy controls, reflected in selective differences in state occupancy and dwell time, we focused on quantifying heterogeneity specifically within the MS cohort. Clustering patients according to OT-based dissimilarities revealed two subgroups with distinct clinical disability and structural disease burden. Crucially, this stratification was not detectable when applying clustering procedures to static functional connectivity, supporting the added value of dynamical features. Our results establish a general methodological framework for extracting clinically relevant phenotypes from temporal brain dynamics, with potential applications across neurological and psychiatric conditions characterized by phenotypic heterogeneity.
articles.author: Taffarello, L., Barzon, G., Mariani, B., Calesella, F., Gallo, A., Altieri, M., De Rosa, A. P., D'Ambrosio, A., Esposito, F., De Marchi, S., Vallesi, A., Allegra, M., Bertoldo, A., Suweis, S., Zorzi, M.

articles.title: Latent state selection, not outcome integration, resolves approach-avoidance conflict
articles.content: Appropriate action selection under approach-avoidance is crucial for survival and emotional resilience. Tasks designed to measure this conflict typically observe response rates at an intermediate rate. However, whether this reflects a single compromised policy or alternation between opposing strategies is unresolved. We trained rats on a novel three trial operant conflict task and recorded anterior insular cortex (aIC) activity with fiber photometry. Fitting a cross-validated GLM-HMM to trial-by-trial choices identified three discrete latent states: a risk-taking state in which rats responded on most conflict trials, a risk-averse state in which they withheld on most conflict trials, and a perseverative state. Rather than integrating the two possible outcomes in conflict, aIC activity flexibly adjusted according to the active state, such that it resembled reward trials in the risk-taking state and punishment trials in the risk-averse state. We also found that acute alcohol increased punished responses by shifting state occupancy. In a yoked Pavlovian cohort, anticipatory aIC signals were reduced, indicating that this encoding requires instrumental agency. Together, these findings suggest that approach-avoidance conflict is resolved by selection between discrete strategies, and that insular recruitment of this process depends on the capacity to act.
articles.author: Marchant, N. J., Pieterse, N. H. J., Sonsini, G., McDonald, A. J., van Mourik, Y., Schetters, D., De Vries, T.

articles.title: Influence of Memory Modulation on Affective States in Methamphetamine Use Disorder
articles.content: Background: Negative affect and low positive affect are linked to craving and relapse in methamphetamine use disorder (MUD). Brief positive autobiographical memory recall improves mood in non-clinical samples, but it has not been tested in people in treatment for MUD. We tested whether positive memory recall improves affective state, withdrawal and craving compared with a neutral recall condition. Methods: Adults with past-year MUD in their first year of abstinence were recruited from two residential treatment programs in Tulsa, Oklahoma. Participants were randomized, blinded to condition, to recall personally meaningful positive memories (Positive; n = 37) or emotionally neutral procedural memories (Procedural; n = 36) during a laboratory session. Positive and negative affect (PANAS, the prespecified primary outcomes), withdrawal (AWQ), craving (visual digital scale; Stimulant Craving Questionnaire), and anhedonia (SHAPS) were assessed before and approximately one hour after the recall. Group x Time effects were tested with mixed ANCOVAs adjusted for sex and age, with Holm and false discovery rate correction. Baseline-adjusted end-of-session differences were estimated for each outcome. Results: Of 80 randomized participants, 73 began the session and were analyzed. The Group x Time interaction was not significant for positive affect (p = .689) or negative affect (p = .399). Baseline-adjusted end-of-session differences were small and imprecise (positive affect: -0.53 points, 95% CI -2.60 to 1.53; negative affect: 0.54 points, 95% CI -0.90 to 1.99). Across both groups, negative affect, withdrawal, craving and desire to use decreased over the session, while positive affect also declined (all p [≤] .015). No secondary or exploratory outcome differed between conditions. Conclusions: A single positive autobiographical memory recall did not produce a detectable end-of-session difference in affect, withdrawal or craving relative to neutral recall in individuals with MUD. Affective and craving states shifted across the session regardless of memory content. Future work should test repeated or more intensive positive-affect interventions in this population.
articles.author: Qundes, S. I., Stewart, J. L., Ironside, M., Paulus, M. P., Gueguen, M. C. M.
